title: HIV and development

blocks.heading: HIV and development
blocks.text: HIV-related illness can affect work, household care and public resources in Namibia and other SADC economies, while effective care improves opportunities to remain well and participate. Accessible testing, treatment and support form part of a public-health response. Avoid treating HIV status as incapacity or using a fictional illness series as actual national prevalence evidence.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Economic pathways
blocks.text:
Illness or premature death can reduce available labour, increase caring work and divert household resources. Treatment access and support can reduce these burdens; stigma and exclusion can add avoidable economic costs independently of health status.

Applied example: Illness can reduce paid working hours and income. Caring responsibilities can reduce another household member’s time for work or education.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: System responses
blocks.text:
HIV responses can combine prevention information, confidential testing, ongoing treatment, maternal-child services and community support. Continuity, trained services and non-stigmatising access matter. Individual treatment decisions belong with qualified health professionals, not a classroom model answer.

Applied example: Confidential testing and continued professional care support timely access to services. Accurate education and community support can reduce misinformation and barriers to participation.

blocks.heading: Follow the mechanism
blocks.text: A fictional household loses paid hours during a period of illness and spends savings on care and transport. A second adult’s caring responsibilities can reduce earnings further. Accessible professional services and income support may reduce some pressures, but the particular household’s circumstances matter. Do not infer an individual’s health or ability to work from an HIV diagnosis alone.

blocks.heading: Use accurate HIV language
blocks.text: [WHO’s HIV fact sheet](https://www.who.int/en/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hiv-aids), checked 20 October 2026, explains that treatment can control HIV and that ordinary contact such as sharing food does not transmit it. Do not use a diagnosis as a reason to exclude someone from schooling or work. This lesson does not prescribe individual treatment.
